questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The total number of bones present in the axial skeleton and appendicular skeleton in an adult human being is ______ and ______, respectively.
questions.explanation: In the adult, 80 bones are present in the axial skeleton, and 126 bones in the appendicular skeleton.
questions.structuredExplanationText: In the adult, 80 bones are present in the axial skeleton, and 126 bones in the appendicular skeleton.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding bones is false?

options.text: Osteocytes are the major cell type in mature bone
Collagen is synthesized in bone by osteoblasts
Bone mainly contains type 2 collagen fibres
Calcium phosphate is the major inorganic mineral

questions.correctAnswerText: Bone mainly contains type 2 collagen fibres
questions.explanation:
Bone mainly contains type 1 collagen fibres. Bones are made up of mineralized collagenous extracellular matrix around specialized cells.

The extracellular matrix is composed of: organic component—around 30% of the organic matrix of bone is made up of collagen, mainly type 1 collagen; inorganic component—the major inorganic mineral in the bone matrix is calcium phosphate in the form of microcrystalline hydroxyapatite.

The specialized cells are: osteoblasts—responsible for synthesis, deposition, and mineralization of bone matrix; collagen is synthesized in bone by osteoblasts and osteoblasts become osteocytes after embedding in matrix. Osteocytes are the major cell type of mature bone, distributed throughout the matrix, and have lost the ability to divide or secrete new matrix. Osteoclasts are responsible for local removal of bone during bone growth and remodelling.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following is a modified long bone?
questions.explanation:
The clavicle is a modified long bone, as it has a modified shaft and no medullary cavity.

Typical long bones have an elongated shaft (diaphysis) and two expanded ends (epiphysis); the shaft has a central medullary cavity and a nutrient foramen directed away from the growing end. Examples include humerus, ulna, radius, femur, tibia and fibula.

Miniature long bones contain only one epiphysis, e.g. metacarpals, metatarsals and phalanges. Modified long bones have a modified shaft or ends and no medullary cavity, e.g. clavicle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following is not a sesamoid bone?
questions.explanation:
Os trigonum is an accessory bone, not a sesamoid bone.

Accessory bones, also known as supernumerary bones, are not always present. They may arise due to an ununited epiphysis developed from extra ossification centres and may be mistaken clinically for fractures.

Examples: Os trigonum—uncommon accessory bone behind the talus, also called lateral tubercle of talus. Os vesalianum—uncommon accessory bone proximal to the fifth metatarsal and found within the peroneus brevis tendon, also known as tuberosity of the fifth metatarsal.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a pneumatic bone?
questions.explanation:
The maxilla is a pneumatic bone.

Pneumatic bones contain air-filled cavities, making them lightweight; they also aid resonance of sound and act as air-conditioning chambers for inspired air. Examples include maxilla, sphenoid and ethmoid.

Short bones include carpal and tarsal bones. Flat bones include sternum, ribs, scapula and bones of the skull vault. Irregular bones include hip bones, vertebrae and bones in the base of the skull.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following accurately describes fabella?
questions.explanation:
Fabella is a sesamoid bone. The term describes a bone embedded within a tendon or muscle. It is a normal anatomic variant present in 10% to 30% of individuals and is found within the tendon of the lateral head of gastrocnemius, where it moves over the lateral femoral condyle.

Important sesamoid bones: patella—the largest sesamoid bone in the quadriceps femoris tendon; pisiform—in flexor carpi ulnaris; fabella—in the lateral head of gastrocnemius; two sesamoids at the first metacarpal within tendons of flexor pollicis brevis and adductor pollicis; two sesamoids at the first metatarsophalangeal articulation within the double tendon of flexor hallucis brevis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding long bones?

options.text: Cancellous bone is absent in the epiphysis
Cancellous bone is present in the outer cortex
Haversian system is absent in cancellous bone
Compact bone has lamellae arranged in a meshwork

questions.correctAnswerText: Haversian system is absent in cancellous bone
questions.explanation:
The Haversian system is seen in compact bone, not cancellous bone.

Compact bones are composed of cylindrical structural units called Haversian systems or osteons. Each contains a central canal with small blood vessels, nerves and endosteum, surrounded by multiple lamellae of calcified matrix containing type I collagen fibres; these canals communicate through Volkmann's canals.

The lamellae of cancellous/spongy bone are arranged in a meshwork and do not form Haversian systems. The diaphysis and outer cortex of long bones are predominantly compact bone, while the epiphysis and inner medulla are predominantly cancellous bone.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 16-year-old boy presented to your OPD with progressive swelling and worsening knee pain over the past 2 months. An X-ray reveals the following finding. Which of the following is true regarding the layer of bone involved?

options.text: Progenitor cells are present in the outer fibrous layer
It is continuous with the capsule of the joint
It is devoid of nerve supply

questions.correctAnswerText: It is continuous with the capsule of the joint
questions.explanation:
The X-ray shows Codman's triangle, due to an irregular periosteal reaction commonly seen in osteosarcoma. The periosteum is a thick fibrous membrane covering the outer surface of all bones except joint surfaces and tendon/ligament insertion points (entheses). At the articular margin, the periosteum is continuous with the joint capsule.

The periosteum has two layers: outer fibrous layer containing fibroblasts; inner cambium/osteogenic layer containing progenitor cells that develop into osteoblasts. It is nourished by periosteal arteries and has a rich nerve supply, making it the most sensitive part of bone.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following structures do the Sharpey's fibers connect?
questions.explanation:
Sharpey's fibers are thick collagen fibers that connect the periosteum to the underlying bone.

They are present in bone and teeth: in bone they tether periosteum to underlying bone; in teeth they connect cementum to the periosteum of the alveolar bone (tooth socket).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following bones develops through intramembranous ossification?
questions.explanation:
Frontal bones undergo intramembranous ossification; the other listed bones undergo enchondral ossification.

Membranous (dermal) bones form through intramembranous ossification, with direct bone formation in highly vascular mesenchymal membranes; examples include frontal, lacrimal, zygomatic and nasal bones. Cartilaginous bones form by intra-cartilaginous/enchondral ossification of a preformed hyaline cartilage model; examples include bones of limbs, vertebral column and thoracic cage. Membranocartilaginous bones ossify from both cartilage and mesenchymal condensation; examples include clavicle, mandible, occipital bone, temporal bone and sphenoid bone.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The structure that the marked muscle in the gluteal region inserts into has ____ type of epiphysis?
questions.explanation:
The marked muscle is piriformis and inserts at the greater trochanter of the femur, which is a traction epiphysis.

Traction epiphysis is nonarticular and does not transmit weight. It provides attachment to one or more tendons exerting traction on the epiphysis. Examples include greater and lesser tubercles of humerus and greater and lesser trochanters of femur.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: While assessing a child with short stature, the senior resident orders an X-ray to better evaluate the structure marked X in the radiograph. Which of the following is a true statement regarding this structure?

options.text: It is made of elastic cartilage
It is supplied only by epiphyseal arteries
It is the site for enchondral ossification

questions.correctAnswerText: It is the site for enchondral ossification
questions.explanation:
The structure marked X is the epiphyseal plate. It is the site for enchondral ossification mainly responsible for growth of long bones.

The epiphyseal/growth plate is a hyaline-cartilage layer separating epiphysis from metaphysis. It receives nourishment from both epiphyseal and metaphyseal arteries. Fractures involving epiphyseal plates are Salter-Harris fractures.

Growing ends: upper limb—upper end of humerus and lower ends of radius and ulna; lower limb—lower end of femur and upper end of tibia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: 'The secondary ossification center that appears first, fuses last'. Which of the following bones violates this law?
questions.explanation:
The fibula violates the law of ossification stating that the secondary ossification center that appears first is the last to fuse.

The secondary ossification center at the lower end of the fibula appears before the upper-end center and fuses before the upper end.

Primary centers appear before birth, usually during late embryonic or early fetal life (seventh week to fourth month), and form the diaphysis. Secondary centers usually appear after birth and form the epiphysis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following parts of the bone is not nourished by the nutrient artery?
questions.explanation:
The nutrient artery does not nourish the outer one-third of the cortex.

The nutrient artery enters the bone shaft through the nutrient foramen and runs obliquely through the cortex. Nutrient arteries of long bones are directed away from the dominant growing epiphysis because the growing bone might pull and rupture the artery. The source mnemonic is: 'To the elbow, I go, from the knee I flee.'

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: In which of the following parts of the bone are hairpin bends of end arteries abundantly present?
questions.explanation:
Hairpin bends of end arteries are seen abundantly in the metaphysis.

The metaphysis is the portion of a long bone between epiphysis and diaphysis. It is the zone of active growth and is highly vascular. Before epiphysial fusion, it is richly supplied through end arteries forming hairpin bends.

The metaphysis is the most common location for osteomyelitis in children because bacteria or emboli are easily trapped in these hairpin bends.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding cartilage is false?
questions.explanation:
Articular cartilage, despite being a type of hyaline cartilage, lacks perichondrium.

Cartilage is connective tissue composed of chondrocytes and fibers (collagen or yellow elastic fibers) embedded in a firm gel-like mucopolysaccharide-rich matrix. It is more elastic than bone, has no blood vessels or lymphatics, and chondrocytes are nourished by diffusion. Cartilage has no nerves and is insensitive.

There are three types: hyaline, elastic and fibrocartilage. Hyaline cartilage except articular cartilage, and elastic cartilage, have perichondrium; fibrocartilage does not.

questions.explanation:
The septal nasal cartilage has hyaline cartilage and not yellow (elastic) cartilage.

Elastic/yellow cartilage contains a matrix rich in fine yellow elastic fibers containing elastin. It is present in apices of arytenoid, epiglottis, corniculate cartilages, cuneiform cartilages, Eustachian tube, pinna (auricle), and external auditory meatus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: What is the type of cartilage found in the structure marked X in the following radiograph?
questions.explanation:
The structure marked X is the pubic symphysis and the cartilage is fibrocartilage.

Fibrocartilage contains a mixture of white fibrous tissue and cartilaginous tissue, making it extremely tough and resilient. Sites include pubic symphysis, manubriosternal joint, articular discs of temporomandibular and sternoclavicular joints, anulus fibrosus of intervertebral discs, menisci of knee, acetabular labrum, glenoid labrum, and lining of bony grooves for tendons.

questions.question: In which of the following cartilages is type I collagen predominantly seen?
questions.explanation: Fibrocartilage predominantly contains type I collagen. Hyaline and elastic cartilages mainly contain type II collagen.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Ligamentum flavum has high levels of:
questions.explanation:
Ligamentum flavum has high levels of elastin fibres.

The ligamenta flava are ligaments connecting the ventral parts of the laminae of adjacent vertebrae. They predominantly contain elastic tissue and form part of the posterior surface of the vertebral canal. Their high elastin content allows stretching by 80% without damage. They resist separation of laminae in flexion and assist extension back to anatomical position.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a fibrous joint?
questions.explanation: The symphysis is not a fibrous joint, but a secondary cartilaginous joint.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: What are synovial joints functionally classified as?
questions.explanation:
Synovial joints are freely movable joints and are therefore functionally classified as diarthroses.

Functional classification: synarthroses are immovable, e.g. fibrous joints; amphiarthroses are slightly mobile, e.g. cartilaginous joints; diarthroses are freely mobile, e.g. synovial joints.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following accurately describes a joint with three or more articular surfaces?
questions.explanation:
A joint with three or more articular surfaces is classified as a compound joint.

Classification by number of articulating surfaces: simple joints have 2 surfaces (e.g. shoulder, hip); compound joints have 3 or more surfaces (e.g. elbow, wrist); complex joints have an intra-articular disc between articular surfaces dividing the joint space (e.g. temporomandibular and sternoclavicular joints).

questions.question: Which of the following joints is known as a peg-and-socket joint?
questions.explanation:
Gomphosis (dentoalveolar syndesmosis) is a peg-and-socket joint between a tooth and its socket.

Fibrous joints are joints where bones are joined by fibrous tissue and are classified as sutures, syndesmosis and gomphosis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: What type of joint is an incudostapedial joint?
questions.explanation:
The incudostapedial joint is a ball-and-socket type of joint.

In ball-and-socket joints a globular head (male surface) fits a cup-shaped socket (female surface). They are multiaxial and allow flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, medial rotation, lateral rotation and circumduction. Examples include shoulder, hip, talocalcaneonavicular and incudostapedial joints.

Note: the other joint between incus and malleus (incudomalleolar joint) is a saddle joint.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 47-year-old lady diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis presented to the clinic with the following deformity. The joint involved in this condition is an example of ________.
questions.explanation:
The deformity shown is hallux valgus, caused by excessive lateral deviation at the first metatarsophalangeal joint. It is an example of an ellipsoid joint.

Ellipsoid joints have an oval convex (male) surface fitting an elliptical concave (female) surface and show biaxial flexion-extension and abduction-adduction; combined movements produce circumduction, while movement around a third axis is prevented by articular shape. Examples include wrist/radiocarpal, atlanto-occipital, metacarpophalangeal and metatarsophalangeal joints.

questions.question: The talocalcaneonavicular joint is a ________ type of joint.
questions.explanation:
The talocalcaneonavicular joint is a ball-and-socket joint.

The ball is the rounded head of talus. The socket is formed by the posterior surface of navicular, anterior articular surface of calcaneus, and upper surface of the plantar calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Forward and backward movements of the mandible that occur at the temporomandibular joint is called as ______ and ______, respectively.
questions.explanation:
Forward and backward movement of the mandible at the temporomandibular joints are protraction and retraction, respectively. Protraction pushes the lower jaw forward; retraction pulls it backward.

Protraction and retraction also occur in the scapula: protraction moves the scapula laterally and anteriorly along the chest wall, while retraction brings it back after protraction.

Opposition brings the thumb tip into contact with a fingertip; return is reposition. Excursion is side-to-side movement of the mandible. Depression and elevation are downward and upward movements of mandible or scapula, respectively.

questions.question: All of the following are rounded or irregular elevations of bones, except ________.
questions.explanation:
The styloid process is a sharp elevation of bone.

Rounded or irregular elevations include tubercle, tuberosity, epicondyle, malleolus and trochanter. Sharp elevations include styloid process, spine, cornu (horn) and hamulus (hook-like).

The marked joint is the costotransverse joint, which is a synovial joint.

The interchondral joint between the costal cartilages of the ninth and tenth ribs is never synovial and is usually absent.
